entities.name: Conon of Bidana
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Conon of Bidana (b. 101 CE, d. 250 CE) was a pivotal, though controversial, figure in the early development of Jewish Christianity, leading a distinct community in the Transjordan region during the 2nd and early 3rd centuries CE. His teachings, characterized by a unique synthesis of Jewish law and nascent Christian beliefs, represented a significant branch within the diverse landscape of post-apostolic religious movements, challenging the emerging orthodoxies of both Rabbinic Judaism and Pauline Christianity. His leadership in establishing a self-sustaining religious community also marks him as an influential organizer, intertwining spiritual guidance with practical community management in an age of profound religious flux.

Active primarily in the region east of the Jordan River, Conon established a self-sustaining community often identified by later Church Fathers as a variant of Ebionitism or a related Judaeo-Christian sect. His followers adhered strictly to Mosaic Law, including circumcision and dietary regulations, while acknowledging Jesus as the Messiah, though generally denying his divine pre-existence and virgin birth. Conon's organizational acumen likely extended to the economic management of his community, given his identification as an 'entrepreneur or business leader,' ensuring its material sustenance and the propagation of its distinct theological tenets amidst the Roman provincial administration and the broader Christian diaspora.
